title: BRUCK SYNDROME 2
alt_titles: OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA WITH CONGENITAL JOINT CONTRACTURES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Bruck syndrome-2 (BRKS2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PLOD2 gene on chromosome 3q23-q24.

checks.claim: Bruck syndrome-2 (BRKS2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PLOD2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Two probands were found with a homozygous frameshift mutation in the alternative exon 13a of PLOD2, indicating that specific inactivation of the longer protein isoform encoded by this gene is sufficient to cause BS.
checks.explanation: Homozygous mutations cause BS; compound heterozygous mutations were also found in a brother with mild BS.

checks.claim: The PLOD2 gene is located on chromosome 3q23-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: two mutations in the lysyl hydroxylase 2 gene (PLOD2, 3q23-q24) have been identified in BS

paragraphs.text: Bruck syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder in which skeletal changes resembling osteogenesis imperfecta, including osteopenia and bone fragility with multiple fractures, occur together with congenital contractures of the large joints (Ha-Vinh et al., 2004). Mutations in PLOD2 cause a range of autosomal recessive connective tissue disorders within the Bruck syndrome-osteogenesis imperfecta phenotypic spectrum (Puig-Hervas et al., 2012).

checks.explanation: OI-like skeletal changes are stated generally; osteopenia and multiple fractures are described only in the reported patient.

checks.claim: In Bruck syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta-like skeletal changes occur together with congenital contractures of the large joints.

checks.explanation: This is the paper's title, restated.

paragraphs.text: Ha-Vinh et al. (2004) reported a boy with Bruck syndrome who had congenital contractures with pterygia at birth and severe osteogenesis imperfecta-like osteopenia and multiple fractures. The authors noted that the combination of pterygia with bone fragility suggested that telopeptide lysyl hydroxylation is involved in prenatal joint formation and morphogenesis.

paragraphs.text: Puig-Hervas et al. (2012) reported 2 brothers with compound heterozygous PLOD2 mutations, one of whom had mild autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta and the other mild Bruck syndrome, as well as a patient with autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta due to a homozygous PLOD2 mutation, and concluded that PLOD2 mutations are associated with autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta phenotypes of variable severity in addition to Bruck syndrome.

paragraphs.text: In the boy with Bruck syndrome reported by Ha-Vinh et al. (2004), urine contained high amounts of hydroxyproline but low amounts of collagen crosslink degradation products. The authors suggested that urinary collagen degradation products and PLOD2 mutation analysis may be used to diagnose Bruck syndrome and to distinguish it from osteogenesis imperfecta.

paragraphs.text: Bruck syndrome-2 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, as shown by homozygous PLOD2 mutation in an affected boy (Ha-Vinh et al., 2004) and by homozygous and compound heterozygous PLOD2 mutations in patients from consanguineous families (Puig-Hervas et al., 2012).

checks.explanation: Homozygous PLOD2 mutation in the boy (BS type 2 = PLOD2-caused).

paragraphs.text: Bank et al. (1999) performed a genome screen in a family with Bruck syndrome and identified a single region on chromosome 17p12 in which all affected sibs shared a cluster of haplotypes identical by descent, suggesting this as a Bruck syndrome locus. Ha-Vinh et al. (2004) referred to Bruck syndrome linked to this region as Bruck syndrome type 1 and to Bruck syndrome caused by PLOD2 mutations as type 2, noting that the proportion of cases of each type was uncertain.

paragraphs.text: In 2 probands from consanguineous Bruck syndrome families, Puig-Hervas et al. (2012) found a homozygous frameshift mutation in the alternative exon 13a of PLOD2, indicating that specific inactivation of the longer PLOD2 protein isoform is sufficient to cause Bruck syndrome. By homozygosity mapping followed by a candidate gene approach, they identified a homozygous donor splice site mutation in PLOD2 in a patient with autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta. Screening of additional samples revealed compound heterozygous PLOD2 mutations in 2 brothers, one with mild autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta and the other with mild Bruck syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bank et al. (1999) found that in Bruck syndrome, lysine residues within the telopeptides of type I collagen in bone were underhydroxylated, leading to aberrant crosslinking, whereas lysine residues in the triple helix were normally modified; cartilage and ligament showed normal crosslinking patterns. They proposed that collagen crosslinking is regulated by tissue-specific enzymes that hydroxylate only telopeptide lysine residues. van der Slot et al. (2003) identified PLOD2 as a putative telopeptide lysyl hydroxylase through the finding of PLOD2 mutations in Bruck syndrome, and found that PLOD2 mRNA was highly increased in fibroblasts from fibrotic skin of patients with systemic sclerosis, whose deposited matrix contained increased pyridinoline crosslinks.

checks.evidence_quote: but that the lysine residues in the triple helix are normally modified

checks.evidence_quote: In contrast to bone, cartilage and ligament show unaltered telopeptide hydroxylation as evidenced by normal patterns of crosslinking.

checks.evidence_quote: collagen crosslinking is regulated primarily by tissue-specific enzymes that hydroxylate only telopeptide lysine residues and not those destined for the helical portion of the molecule
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. The paper says "regulated primarily", a slightly stronger qualifier than the draft's wording.

agent.process_note: All 4 papers are available only as abstracts, and I read each one in full. The causal gene (PLOD2) and its 3q23-q24 location come from the abstracts of Ha-Vinh et al. (2004) and van der Slot et al. (2003). No gene MIM number was supplied, so I left it out. The abstracts give no exact nucleotide changes for any variant, and none for the Puig-Hervas frameshift or splice mutations. The names G601V and T608I come from Ha-Vinh et al. citing earlier work, not from the van der Slot abstract. The abstracts don't say whether the Ha-Vinh patient's parents were related or what his ancestry was. Bank et al. (1999) describes the chromosome 17p12 (BRKS1) family, so I used it only for heterogeneity and pathogenesis.
